'''''Trimezia''''' is a [[genus]] of [[flowering plant]]s in the family [[Iridaceae]], native to the warmer parts of southern [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], [[South America]], [[Florida]], and the [[West Indies]].<ref name=g>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=325236 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref> ''Trimezia'' is placed in the tribe [[Trimezieae]]. The division of the tribe into genera has varied considerably. In one approach, it contains only the genus ''Trimezia'', which then includes the genera '''''Neomarica''''', '''''Pseudotrimezia''''' and '''''Pseudiris'''''. In other approaches, two to five genera are recognized, sometimes also including the genus '''''Deluciris'''''.

The English names '''walking iris''', '''apostle's iris''' and '''apostle plant''' have been used for many species, regardless of the generic placement (e.g. for ''[[Trimezia gracilis]]'', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Neomarica gracilis''). New plantlets form at the end of the flower spikes; after flowering, the spikes fall over and a new plant grows, so the plant "walks". Names including "apostle" refer to the incorrect belief that plants do not flower until 12 or more leaves are present.<ref name=Klin10/>

==Description==
The rootstock is variously described as an elongated corm or a rhizome. Plants vary in height from about {{convert|7|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} in the case of ''T. pusilla'' to {{convert|1.6|m|ft|abbr=on|1}} in the case of ''T. spathata'' subsp. ''sincorana''. Linear to lanceolate leaves grow from the base of the plant. Most species have flowers in some shade of yellow. The six [[tepal]]s are arranged in two series. The outer tepals ([[sepal]]s) are larger than the inner ones ([[petal]]s); both may have brown-purple markings at the base. The [[stamen]]s have free filaments (i.e. they not fused together or fused to the style). The [[Gynoecium|style]] is divided into three branches, each of which usually has two lobes.<ref name=Inne85>{{Citation |last=Innes |first=Clive |year=1985 |title=The World of Iridaceae |publication-place=Ashington, UK |publisher=Holly Gate International |isbn=978-0-948236-01-3 }}, pp. 375–379</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The genus ''Trimezia'' was first published with an appropriate description by [[William Herbert (botanist)|William Herbert]] in 1844.<ref name=IPNI_30021684-2/> Herbert attributed the name to [[Richard Anthony Salisbury|Salisbury]], whose use he described as "{{lang|la|absque charactere}}" ('without character').<ref name=Herb44/> The genus name is derived from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] words {{lang|grc|τρεῖς}}, {{Transliteration|grc|treis}}, meaning 'three' and {{lang|grc|μείζων}}, {{Transliteration|grc|meizon}}, meaning 'greater', referring to the outer three tepals being much larger than the inner three.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hyam |first=R. |last2=Pankhurst |first2=R.J. |year=1995 |title=Plants and their names : a concise dictionary |publication-place=Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-866189-4 |name-list-style=amp }} p. 505.</ref>

''Trimezia'' is placed in the tribe Trimezieae of the subfamily Iridoideae.<ref name=LovoWinkGilAmar18/> The number of genera into which the tribe is divided has varied considerably. Three genera were used before 2008: ''Trimezia'', ''Neomarica'' and ''Pseudotrimezia''. Some sources used all three; others combined ''Trimezia'' and ''Neomarica'' but retained ''Pseudotrimezia''.<ref name=LovoWinkGilAmar18/> A further genus, ''Pseudiris'', was published in 2008. [[Molecular phylogenetics|Molecular phylogenetic]] studies have shown that although the tribe is [[Monophyly|monophyletic]], the genera as traditionally used, based on morphological characteristics, are not. Three of the four main [[Cladistics|clades]] found in these analyses combine species from more than one genus.<ref name=LovoWinkMell12/><ref name=LovoWinkGilAmar18/> One response to these findings, adopted {{As of|2025|February|lc=yes}} by [[Plants of the World Online]], is to combine genera; thus ''Deluciris'', ''Neomarica'', ''Pseudiris'' and ''Pseudotrimezia'' are all placed within ''Trimezia''.<ref name=POWO_30021684-2/> An alternative approach, retaining the traditional genera but with changed [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscriptions]], was put forward in 2018; an additional new genus, ''[[Deluciris]]'', was also created within the tribe.<ref name=LovoWinkGilAmar18/>

===Distinction between genera===
When ''Trimezia'' was distinguished from ''Neomarica'' prior to molecular phylogenetic studies, i.e. entirely on morphological grounds, some vegetative characters were considered diagnostic. ''Trimezia'' in this sense always grows from [[corm]]s, ''Neomarica'' almost always from [[rhizome]]s. ''Trimezia'' has flowering stems ([[Scape (botany)|scapes]]) that are circular in cross-section, whereas ''Neomarica'' has flattened scapes.<ref name=ChukGiul01>{{Citation |last1=Chukr |first1=Nadia Said |last2=Giulietti |first2=Ana Maria |year=2001 |title=New combinations in the genus ''Neomarica'' (Iridaceae) and its segregation from ''Trimezia'' on the basis of morphological features |journal=Novon |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=376–380 |url=http://www.botanicus.org/page/642439 |access-date=2012-05-07 |name-list-style=amp |doi=10.2307/3393147|jstor=3393147 }}</ref> Lovo et al. (2018) consider these characteristics to be among those distinguishing their circumscription of ''Neomarica'' from the other genera into which they divide the tribe.<ref name=LovoWinkGilAmar18/>

{{As of|2025|February}}, [[Plants of the World Online]] accepted about 80 species of ''Trimezia''.<ref name=POWO_30021684-2/> However, this includes species that other sources place in different genera in the tribe Trimezieae. The placement in Lovo et al. (2018), where given in their paper, is shown in the second column.

==Distribution and habitat==
The genus is native to the warmer parts of southern [[Mexico]], [[Central America]], [[South America]], [[Florida]], and parts of the [[West Indies]].<ref name=POWO_30021684-2/> ''Trimezia'' species typically grow in damp grassland.<ref name=ChukGiul08/>
